restatements.text: Names the measure the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Establishes the short title as the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.

Finds that federal and state funding cuts threaten health care, education, and food programs in California, while billionaires pay lower effective tax rates on wealth than average earners, justifying a one-time 5% tax on billionaire wealth to backfill these programs.
States the purpose is to protect healthcare, education, and food assistance by raising revenue through a one-time tax on billionaires to address urgent funding reductions.

Amends the California Constitution to authorize a one-time tax on the wealth of California billionaires, creating the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund. Allocates 90% of the fund to health care and 10% to education and food assistance. Exempts the fund from existing General Fund definitions and appropriations limits, prohibits borrowing or transferring these funds, and allows facial legal challenges without first paying the tax.

Creates the Reserve Fund in the Government Code, specifying expenditures for Medi-Cal, K-14 education, and food assistance programs. Allows the Legislature to appropriate up to $22.5 billion annually for health and $2.5 billion for education and food. Requires annual financial reporting and a start-up loan of up to $50 million to the Franchise Tax Board.
Adds the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act to the Revenue and Taxation Code.

Imposes a 5% excise tax for the 2026 tax year on the net worth of individuals and trusts with $1 billion or more in wealth. Provides a phased reduction for net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, establishes payment installment options, requires filing declarations, and grants the Franchise Tax Board audit powers.

Defines which debts and liabilities reduce a taxpayer's net worth, allowing recourse debts and sole proprietorship debts, but excluding certain non-recourse debts, non-arm's length debts, entity-level debts where the taxpayer lacks personal liability, and post-October 2025 charitable pledges.

Defines methods for determining the fair market value of assets, establishes a formula based on book value and profits for valuing business interests, exempts directly held real estate and retirement accounts from the tax base, and requires certified appraisals for other assets over $1 million.
Creates Optional Deferral Accounts that allow taxpayers lacking liquid assets to defer their tax obligations, while imposing taxes on material distributions or withdrawals from those accounts.

Requires appraisers to submit copies of certified appraisals to the state tax board, directs the board to adopt detailed rules for appraisals, and allows the board to penalize appraisers for substantial valuation errors.

Sets the rule that 100 percent of the tax is apportioned to California for residents, while allowing taxpayers to petition for an alternative apportionment if they can prove their wealth was not substantially accumulated or sustained in the state.
Allows a credit against the California wealth tax for a pro rata share of similar net wealth taxes paid to other jurisdictions.
Defines terms used throughout the measure, including setting January 1, 2026, as the date for determining residency and December 31, 2026, as the valuation date.

Grants the Franchise Tax Board authority to administer the tax and adopt regulations, exempts these rules from the Administrative Procedure Act until 2028, and sets a ten-year window to issue deficiency assessments for 2026.
Allows the Legislature to amend the measure by a two-thirds vote, provided the changes are consistent with and further its purposes.
Provides that if any part of the measure is invalidated by a court, the remaining parts stay in effect, and directs courts to adjust dates if needed to preserve the tax.

Establishes penalties of 20 percent and 40 percent for understating the tax owed, authorizes the Board to disregard transactions lacking economic substance, allows the Board to hire outside experts, and provides a six-month filing extension for 2026.
Directs that the measure be liberally construed to effectuate its purposes.
Creates an expedited validation process in Sacramento County Superior Court to determine the measure's legality, with direct appeals to the California Supreme Court and target dates for resolution.
Prohibits taxpayers from deducting the state net worth tax from their state income taxes.
States that if this measure receives more votes than a competing net worth tax measure on the same ballot, its provisions will override the competing measure.

Authorizes the state, the measure's proponent, or any citizen to sue or intervene to defend the legality of the measure, providing for the payment of reasonable attorney fees from state funds if the Attorney General does not defend it.

evidence.quote: Debts and other liabilities of a taxpayer’s sole proprietorship shall reduce net worth as if they were debts or other liabilities of the taxpayer. The taxpayer’s net worth shall not be reduced by the amount of debts or other liabilities of a partnership, limited liability company, or other business entity (other than a sole proprietorship) which are allocated to the taxpayer for purposes of computing tax, except to the extent that the taxpayer is personally liable for such debt or other liability.
evidence.why: It increases tax complexity by requiring debts to be treated differently depending on the specific legal structure of the business holding them.

evidence.quote: the fair market value of those interests at the end of any tax year shall be presumed to be the sum of the book value of the business entity according to generally accepted accounting principles as of the end of the tax year plus a present-value multiplier of 7.5 times the annual book profits of the business entity
evidence.why: It introduces a complex, specific formula involving multipliers to value business interests, making tax calculation more complicated.

evidence.quote: If the Board determines that a transaction or series of transactions lack economic substance, or that a substantial purpose for any transaction or series of transactions was to obtain a tax benefit with respect to this Part that is not intended by the voters or the Legislature, the Board may determine the tax consequences to any person in a manner that is reasonable in light of all the facts and circumstances in order to deny such benefit.
evidence.why: The text increases tax complexity by giving the tax board discretion to retroactively alter the tax consequences of transactions it deems to lack a non-tax business purpose.

evidence.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026 on the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth by applicable individuals with net worth of $1 billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) or more, and on applicable trusts.
evidence.why: It imposes a substantial new tax exclusively on the state's wealthiest individuals.

evidence.quote: No deduction shall be allowed for any tax imposed by the State on net worth, including the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act (Part 27 of this Code) notwithstanding any other provision of law
evidence.why: By prohibiting a deduction for the net worth tax, which applies only to the highest wealth brackets, the text prevents these taxpayers from using it to lower their state income tax burden, maintaining a larger share of taxes from higher incomes.

evidence.quote: Any appraiser making a certified appraisal for the purposes of this Part shall send a copy of that certified appraisal to the Board, along with information sufficient for identifying the taxpayer for whom the certified appraisal was prepared
evidence.why: It requires appraisers to share sensitive valuation and identifying information about clients directly with the tax board.

evidence.quote: The Director of Finance shall transfer to the Franchise Tax Board, as a start-up loan from the Reserve Fund or General Fund, up to $50 million for the first year following passage of this Act for actual and necessary costs in administering its duties under this Act and for evaluating their efficacy.
evidence.why: It expands government regulatory and administrative capacity by funding a new $50 million program within the Franchise Tax Board.

evidence.quote: The Board shall adopt regulations, or publish guidance, further detailing the requirements for certified appraisals and for appraisers qualified to make certified appraisals for purposes of this Chapter.
evidence.why: It expands the regulatory authority of the tax board to set the rules and qualifications for certified appraisals and appraisers.

evidence.quote: Until January 1, 2028, the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to any regulation, standard, criterion, procedure, determination, rule, notice, guideline, or any other guidance established or issued by the Board pursuant to this Part.
evidence.why: The text expands the regulatory power of the tax board by exempting it from standard oversight and procedural rules.

evidence.quote: If the Board determines that a transaction or series of transactions lack economic substance, or that a substantial purpose for any transaction or series of transactions was to obtain a tax benefit with respect to this Part that is not intended by the voters or the Legislature, the Board may determine the tax consequences to any person in a manner that is reasonable in light of all the facts and circumstances in order to deny such benefit.
evidence.why: The text expands the agency's authority to override the form of transactions and assess taxes based on its own determination of economic substance.

evidence.quote: The following categories of assets shall be exempt from all taxation under this part and also from the reporting requirements of this Section: (A) Except as described in subparagraph (B), qualified pensions and individual retirement arrangements
evidence.why: It protects seniors' retirement security by exempting pensions and retirement accounts from the wealth tax base.

evidence.quote: Ninety percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Health Account for health care funding, which may include expenditures to restore or address any reductions in federal funding or state appropriations; investments to protect or enhance Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low-and moderate-income individuals; support for safety net health care providers serving vulnerable populations; preventing or mitigating facility closures or reductions in service levels
evidence.why: It earmarks billions of dollars specifically to fund Medi-Cal, support safety net clinics, and prevent health facility closures.

evidence.quote: for each asset or group of substantially interchangeable assets (such as derivative contracts relating to the same underlying security) worth in excess of $1 million ($1,000,000), the taxpayer shall submit a certified appraisal.
evidence.why: It increases compliance costs by forcing taxpayers to obtain formal, certified appraisals for high-value assets.

evidence.quote: The Legislature shall have the authority to appropriate up to $22.5 billion each fiscal year from the Billionaire Tax Health Account and up to $2.5 billion each year from the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account.
evidence.why: It places the authority to appropriate up to $25 billion annually from the new tax in the hands of the elected state Legislature.

analysis.answer: Current law is not provided. The measure introduces a new one-time 5% excise tax on the net worth of California residents who hold $1 billion or more in wealth.
Direct costs include a $50 million start-up loan to the Franchise Tax Board. There will also be massive compliance costs for billionaires needing highly complex private appraisals of diverse assets.

Individuals and applicable trusts holding over $1 billion in net worth pay the tax. Low-income families, Medi-Cal patients, safety net providers, K-14 schools, and individuals relying on food assistance benefit from the resulting funds.

Targeted individuals are highly incentivized to attempt to relocate their residence, move assets, or use complex trust and corporate structuring to minimize reported net worth. Despite nonsupplantation clauses, the legislature may also find ways to shift standard budgetary spending since massive new reserve funds are available for safety net programs.

The text asserts that state safety nets and schools face severe budget threats from federal funding cuts, occurring alongside unprecedented concentration of wealth. The mechanism addresses this by extracting a one-time fraction of billionaire wealth to securely fund these public programs.

The Franchise Tax Board gains extraordinary administrative and audit discretion over the private wealth of the state's richest residents. The state Legislature gains authority to appropriate tens of billions of dollars annually.

The economic impact of state-level wealth taxes is heavily disputed. Proponents point to studies suggesting such taxes are administratively practical and that evasion can be constrained; critics and other economists argue that wealth taxes trigger massive capital flight, deter investment, are extremely difficult to value accurately, and frequently miss revenue projections.

The measure appropriates a $50 million start-up loan to the Franchise Tax Board just for initial administration and evaluation, indicating substantial initial administrative overhead and enforcement costs.

Because a significant portion of this measure amends the state constitution (Article XIII, Section 37), those provisions cannot be undone or significantly altered without another statewide ballot initiative.

Current law was not provided. The measure establishes detailed valuation methods for assessing net worth, creates Optional Deferral Accounts to delay tax payments, mandates certified appraisals for high-value assets, sets penalties for inaccurate appraisals, and outlines apportionment rules for determining the share of wealth taxable in California.

Compliance costs for taxpayers will be substantial, as they must obtain certified appraisals for assets over $1 million, calculate business values using specified formulas, and track deferral accounts. The state will face administrative costs to adopt regulations, monitor compliance, and resolve apportionment disputes.

Wealthy taxpayers bear the cost of the tax and the compliance burden. The state gains revenue. Owners of real property benefit from an exemption. Appraisers face new risks of financial penalties for valuation errors, which may lead them to charge higher fees.

Taxpayers may shift their investments into exempt assets like real estate or retirement accounts, or temporarily move tangible property out of state. Some may use Optional Deferral Accounts to delay payment. Appraisers may raise their fees or decline to value complex assets due to the risk of state penalties.

The text addresses the difficulty of valuing private businesses and non-liquid assets for a wealth tax. It uses a formula based on book profits, mandates certified appraisals, and provides deferral accounts for those who cannot easily liquidate assets to pay. It attempts to prevent evasion by taxing assets transferred for less than fair market value.
The Franchise Tax Board gains significant authority to issue regulations, define material distributions, determine alternative apportionment methods, and penalize appraisers.

Whether rigid valuation formulas, deferral accounts, and strict apportionment rules can effectively and fairly capture wealth without causing economic distortion or capital flight is disputed by economists and tax researchers.

A notable portion of the revenue will be absorbed by enforcement costs. Auditing business valuations, tracking material distributions from deferral accounts, evaluating certified appraisals, and litigating alternative apportionment petitions will require specialized and intensive administrative effort.
Amendment rules are not specified in these clauses.

Current law, which was not provided, does not detail the administration of a net worth tax. The measure creates these details, directing the Franchise Tax Board to administer the tax, adopt regulations outside standard oversight processes until 2028, and enforce underpayment penalties.

The text creates administrative and enforcement costs for the Franchise Tax Board, which may hire outside experts and counsel. It creates significant compliance costs for taxpayers navigating complex anti-avoidance rules, and potentially heavy litigation costs as the definitions of "economic substance" and the expedited review mechanisms are tested in court.

The costs are borne by applicable high-wealth taxpayers and the state budget (for enforcement and legal defense). The state benefits from the resulting revenue and collected penalties. Appraisers and specialized tax lawyers may see increased demand for their services.

Taxpayers may restructure their assets or attempt to move jurisdictions to avoid the tax and its severe understatement penalties. In response to anti-avoidance rules, they will likely heavily litigate whether their transactions have "economic substance." The Franchise Tax Board will likely issue initial regulations quickly, utilizing its temporary exemption from the Administrative Procedure Act.

The text addresses the problem of delayed implementation and tax avoidance that could undermine the collection of the new tax. It attempts to solve these problems by imposing strict understatement penalties, enabling the tax board to disregard transactions lacking economic substance, and forcing all legal challenges into a single, expedited track to reach final resolution quickly.

The Franchise Tax Board gains significant discretionary power over defining taxable transactions and enforcement. The measure's proponents and any private citizen gain the unusual power to bring legal action to defend the measure at the state's expense.

Researchers disagree on whether strict anti-avoidance rules, exit taxes, and penalties effectively capture targeted wealth. Some studies suggest aggressive enforcement ensures compliance and limits avoidance, while others argue that high compliance costs, complex financial structuring, and capital mobility ultimately allow individuals to shield assets or leave the jurisdiction regardless of these rules.

Substantial resources will be consumed by enforcement and litigation. Applying complex anti-avoidance doctrines, conducting specialized asset appraisals, and managing the expedited validation litigation will require significant state and private legal resources.

It is statutory but includes a restriction: it can only be amended by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and the amendment must be consistent with and further its purposes. Otherwise, it must be undone by another voter initiative.

flags.quote: (viii) Other reductions in federal funding that threaten or cause reductions in Medi-Cal or other health care coverage... or to the health care safety net more generally.
flags.note: Provides a very broad and subjective definition of 'reductions in federal funding'.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth
flags.note: Overrides other constitutional limitations on property taxation.

flags.quote: The Legislature shall have the authority to appropriate up to $22.5 billion each fiscal year from the Billionaire Tax Health Account and up to $2.5 billion each year from the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account.
flags.note: The real-world effect of the tax revenue depends entirely on subsequent annual legislative appropriations.

flags.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026
flags.note: The tax is effective specifically for the 2026 tax year.

flags.quote: Ninety percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Health Account... Ten percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account
flags.note: Bundles healthcare funding, public education funding, and food assistance into a single tax measure.

flags.quote: a facial challenge to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act is authorized to be adjudicated through a validation action under Chapter 6 of Part 27 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, Section 50314 without requiring the payment of the tax claimed to be facially invalid.
flags.note: Explicitly authorizes a private validation action lawsuit without standard exhaustion (payment) requirements.

flags.quote: Any feature of an asset, such as a shareholder rights plan, shall not be taken into account in determining the asset’s value where a significant purpose and effect of adding the feature is to reduce the appraised value of the asset.
flags.note: The phrase "significant purpose and effect" is subjective and open to broad interpretation by tax authorities.

flags.quote: The rules in this Chapter supersede other rules, including the rules concerning the division of income for purposes of part-year residence.
flags.note: Explicitly overrides other existing apportionment and residency rules.

flags.quote: The Board shall adopt regulations, or publish guidance, further detailing the requirements for certified appraisals and for appraisers qualified to make certified appraisals for purposes of this Chapter.
flags.note: The requirements and qualifications for crucial certified appraisals depend on future rules adopted by the board.
Sets specific retroactive or immediate dates for establishing tax residency.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding Section 19057 or any other law, every notice of a proposed deficiency assessment under this part in regards to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and before January 1, 2027, shall be mailed to the taxpayer within ten years after the return was filed.
The Board shall have the authority to adopt regulations to implement, interpret, make specific, or otherwise carry out any provision of this Part.
flags.note: Administration of the complex tax rules relies heavily on future Board regulations.

flags.quote: The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Requires a supermajority and limits amendments to those that "further the purposes" of the act.

flags.quote: The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as “the Act,” are severable. While the Act has been carefully designed to comply with existing law, if any provision of the Act or its application is held invalid, unconstitutional, or otherwise unenforceable, that finding shall not affect the enforceability of other provisions or applications.
